speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that representatives of all the railway unions of Newfoundland are meeting today with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) following a long campaign to have the minister become interested in the preservation and revitalization of the Newfoundland railway, led by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) in Ottawa, and supported by a unanimous resolution passed by the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and by about 100 per cent of all organized bodies and public opinion in Newfoundland, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the fact that the Prime Minister last week, in answering a question, defended Canada's comparative economic progress and referred to Japan's very favourable position as being in great part due to a policy of not laying off workers in periods of recession or stagflation, and in view of the fact that Canada lags far behind not only Japan but many western European countries in this aspect of employees' protection, and in view of the fact that the ideas of corporate social responsibility and workers' job rights remain practically excluded from our labour-management legislation in this country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. That the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour show some leadership on this issue and persuade their provincial counterparts to adopt this type of progressive labour-management relations.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED INEFFICIENCY IN SAFETY PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Over the last two or three years, Canadians have been bombarded virtually daily by horror stories of inefficiency in safety standards in the air, on the water and on the ground. The matter culminated just this week in a further "leaked" report with respect to the difficulties with air inspection and safety measures.
I ask the minister whether this continuing story, that now embraces 18 or 19 serious major incidents in transportation in this country in the last two years, is the result of a breakdown in communications between the minister and his advisers, or is it a fact that the minister has not the time or the inclination to spend in order to ensure that Canadians continue to enjoy the right to safe travel or, equally important, the right to believe they can travel safely. What in hell is going on with transportation safety in this country?

speechtext:

If we have to put up with the high cost of imported food, what about doing something on the domestic front? subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF SUBSIDIES ON CERTAIN FOODS

In terms of the subsidies, there is concern about the expenditure level of the government, and sometimes subsidies benefit at the same time not only the poor but the rich. As was explained in this House not long ago by the Prime Minister, we have increased family allowances for the poor and we have given pensioners more money in order that they may cope with some of these problems. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The AECL is seeking to bid for a second nuclear energy reactor to be supplied to the Argentine.
In light of the fact that the Argentine government has not ratified the non-nuclear proliferation treaty and has so far balked at Canada's demand for full-scale safeguards on a bilateral basis, and in light of the admission by Admiral Madero, president of the NAEC of the Argentine, that the Argentine was contemplating the use of material from the first Canadian reactor sold to them for the reprocessing of material which would be used for nuclear weapons, will the minister give assurances to this House that Canada will not proceed with the sale to the Argentine of further nuclear reactors until full safeguards are secured?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SAFEGUARD PROVISIONS IN SALE OF NUCLEAR REACTORS TO ARGENTINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish, as always, to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. Despite its technical nature, I think I can give him an assurance on the specifics. To be more precise, the agreement we have with Argentina is specific and states that all equipment, material and nuclear material and facilities subject to the agreement- and here I am quoting from it-
-shall be used for peaceful purposes only and shall not be used for the development, manufacture or detonation of any nuclear explosive device.
The second point is that the Argentines may not reprocess any material subject to the agreement without seeking Canada's agreement to do so; and, third, in the event of non-compliance, Canada may suspend co-operation and may request that Argentina immediately cease to use any Canadian supplies. If the hon. member would like me to send him more details, I would be glad to do so.

speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware of the detailed and extensive report recently prepared by the U.S. Comptroller-General for the Congress which stated that "it is not the current United States Policy to convert from the present customary system to the metric system"?
2.	Is the government co-ordinating Canada's metric conversion programme with that in the U.S. in order to minimize any costs and negative effects for our industries and, if not, for what reason?
3.	Is the government aware of a survey in the U.S. Comptroller-General's report showing that 80 per cent of the businesses in the Fortune 500 list did not expect any significant change in exports or imports as a result of the metric conversion?
4.	Has a similar survey been conducted for Canadian businesses and (a) if so, what were the results (b) if not, for what reason?
5.	Is the government considering a moratorium on further metrication in Canada until the positive and negative features can be re-examined in light of changing attitudes towards metrication in the U.S. as reflected in the Comptroller-General's report?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: GAO REPORT-U.S.
speechtext:
1. The General Accounting Office (GAO) Report to the U.S. Congress prepared by the Comptroller General, entitled "Getting a Better Understanding of the Metric System" has been reviewed by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Metric Commission Canada.
As stated in an article on page one of the "Metric Monitor" of December 1978 on this subject:
"The United States Metric Board does not share this opinion"
i.e. that it is not U.S. policy to convert to the metric system.
That the GAO has misinterpreted United States policy is further stated in a letter dated Nov. 27/78 from U.S. Congressman Olin E. Teague, Chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Science and Technology, to Dr. Louis F. Polk, Chairman of the U.S. Metric Board. In his letter Congressman Teague states:
"It has come to my attention that the recently issued GAO report on the Metric System may have caused some misunderstanding of the legislative intent embodied in Public Law 94-168, the Metric Conversion Act of 1975 ... contrary to the analysis in the GAO report. . . this (Act) . . . does, in fact, set forth a clear policy for metric conversion in the United States. That policy is to facilitate the conversion to metric use in our country to reduce the total cost and inconvenience to our people".

February 9, 1979
Order Paper Questions
The full text of this letter is contained in the December 13, 1978 official report of the Proceedings (Issue 17) of the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce in the evidence given by Mr. D. R. B. McArthur, Chairman of the Metric Commission Canada.
2.	Yes. This is the policy being pursued as said out in the White Paper on Metric Conversion in Canada (January 1970), agreed to by the House leaders of all parties.
3.	The GAO report indicated that there are more significant reasons for increasing export markets than a metric changeover such as "competitive prices, high quality, superior technology and good reputation and reliability" but this does not mean metric conversion is not a factor in promoting exports. A majority (66 per cent) of the largest U.S. industrial businesses (the Fortune 500) who responded to GAO's questionnaire believe metric conversion is inevitable and would facilitate trade through a common measurement language. The breakdown of responses to the GAO question as to whether metric conversion will increase or protect the present amount of exports and work overseas is: 27 per cent (agree), 32 per cent (disagree), 23 per cent (does not apply), 18 per cent (no basis to judge).
4.	One of the first activities carried out by Metric Commission Canada in January and February 1972 was to conduct a survey on the expected effects of metric conversion on Canadian businesses. A letter-questionnaire was mailed to about 100 national associations. Seventy-eight associations replied. One of the questions asked was:
"To what extent must your program be planned to take account of developments in metric conversion in the United States"?
(1)	Is this relationship controlling?
(2)	If not, can conversion be undertaken independently of action in the United States?
(a) The response to the 1972 letter-questionnaire was summerized as indicating 62 per cent of the companies responding expected to take into account developments in metric conversion in the U.S. A.
Only 39 per cent of this 62 per cent considered this relationship controlling. A good example of this is automobile manufacturing industry, and the majority of 1979 model year automobile parts are already being manufactured both in Canada and the U.S.A. to metric dimensions. Another example is the aircraft industry and here metric conversion is proceeding slowly.
About 38 per cent considered that metric conversion could be undertaken independently of action in the U.S.A. The Canadian Construction Association, the Canada Grains Council and the Fisheries Council of Canada are a few examples. Many sector plans express the view that metric conversion will assist export sales. For example sector 7.42 Sporting Goods in their metric conversion plan state:

"It is felt that the introduction of SI Units will help the sporting goods industry to become more competitive in countries when metric measures have been established".
The working group on Metric Export-Import Trade (MEXIM) of Metric Commission Canada; which represents all Metric Commission Canada steering committees carried out a study in 1976 which indicated that 45 per cent of Canada's exports are metric sensitive. As a by-product of meetings of the MEXIM trade group a growing number of companies already have been identified as increasing their sales as a result of metric conversion. For instance, as a result of metric export opportunities to the United States, Canadian companies such as Intercomp Resource Development and Engineering Ltd. of Calgary, McGraw-Hill Ryerson Ltd. of Toronto, Spectrum Educational Supplies Ltd. of Markham, Science Research Associates (Canada) Ltd. of Willowdale, and Merlan Scientific Ltd. of Mississauga to name a few have exported for the first time to the United States.
5.	No. The United States is proceeding with their metric conversion program and sector committees in the Canadian program maintain close contact with their U.S. counterparts. The U.S. House of Representatives recently defeated a bill seeking abolition of the U.S. Metric Board and the repeal of the 1975 U.S. Metric Conversion Act by a 4 to 1 margin which is the same margin of those in favour of the passage of the 1975 Metric Conversion Act. The first appropriation for the U.S. Metric Board passed the House of Representatives in 1978 by a 302 to 75 vote. These votes reflect the broad support for the U.S. program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the federal government having taken advantage of the weaknesses of the British North America Act (BNA Act) to infringe on provincial jurisdictions and undermine the sovereignty of the provinces, has failed:
-to leave the initiative of constitutional negotiations to the provinces, in accordance with the spirit of Confederation, by giving them the final say in the decision-making process;
-to discuss the introduction of economic rights for all citizens in a new Constitution;
-as well as to recognize that new constitutional arrangements may be ratified only by the population of the provinces through referendum held in the respective provinces.
[DOT]-Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to move a motion which will interest to the highest degree, I am sure, the House and all members, and which reads as follows, and I quote:
-having taken advantage of the weaknesses of the British North America Act (BNA Act) to infringe on provincial jurisdictions and undermine the sovereignty of the provinces, the federal government has failed:
-to leave the initiative of constitutional negotiations to the provinces, in accordance with the spirit of confederation, by giving them the final say in the decision-making process;
-to discuss the introduction of economic rights for all citizens in a new constitution;
-as well as to recognize that new constitutional arrangements may be ratified only by the population of the provinces through referendums held in the respective provinces.
Mr. Speaker, as this is perhaps the last opportunity we have to put forward such a motion before parliament is dissolved, I think it is a good thing to look back on the road we travelled and even risk a little review on the 112 years of confederation in which we find weaknesses, of course. We are going to examine closely the actions of certain people or governments who took advantage of those weaknesses and even brought them about in order to create a climate of suspicion rather than of co-operation. We will then be suggesting ways which would enable Canadians to live up to their Canadian reality in that harmony which is indispensable to people who need to live side by side with respect and honour.
I want to indicate sincerely that although it is true that all members of the Social Credit Party of Canada now sitting in this House come from Quebec and have been for over a decade the official opposition from that province in Ottawa, the fact still remains that the opposition motion I have the honour to move today is based first and foremost on economic concerns.
Indeed, in the present state of affairs nobody will deny that it is more difficult to introduce economic legislation in Canada than in any other country and that is so because of our two-tier system of government. The problem stems from the fact that

successive federal governments in the past have refused to face reality, and reality is that duality and regionalism have become the predominant features of our Canadian political and economic systems.
Besides, I believe that these past few years all Canadians have been able to witness the omnipresence of those features in federal-provincial conferences. The last one-and it was a typical one in that respect-only resulted in the concurrence in two of the four points on the agenda, namely the questions of family rights and of the monarchy-two minor subjects on which both levels of government had agreed long before the conference. Indeed, the importance of recognizing Canada's duality and regionalism was raised by the Task Force on Canadian Unity in its report entitled A Future Together in the following terms which appear on page 115 of the Pepin-Robarts report and I quote:
Consensus on constitutional patriation and amendment plus a limited number of matters unrelated to Canadian duality and regionalism would not, in our judgment, be a sufficient response to the constitutional implications of the present crisis.
Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the hon. members that this was not said by the Parti Quebecois or by myself, but rather by a study group which was set up by this federal government and which worked for more than 17 months at the cost of $3.5 million to the Canadian taxpayer.
It is unfortunate to have to say this, but it is a fact that every time constitutional issues are discussed, the government can only suggest minor amendments. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this ad hoc approach cannot bring about any longterm solutions. For instance, at the recent federal-provincial conference, the federal government seemed willing to relinquish certain of its powers to the provinces in the field of communications, more particularly as concerns the issuance of permits to cable companies, but the Prime Minister is well aware that what the provinces have been requesting for many years is to be allowed to control program contents since each province has its own special needs. I sincerely believe, Mr. Speaker, that by continuously sticking to such a stand, the government is making this whole country dance on quicksand.
We of the Social Credit Party of Canada believe that the time has come to replace the British North America Act with a new constitution, the first one that the Canadian provinces would establish for themselves, which would include economic rights for all citizens, would be submitted to the approval of the population of each province and would therefore better correspond to the present situation. Indeed, this is what we want to explain today in this House, first of all by proving that the British North America Act is not an obstacle to the enactment of a truly Canadian constitution because this act can be repudiated today by Canada for the same reasons that it should have been in 1867 if we had been more careful. Secondly, we will clearly demonstrate the central government's
February 9, 1979

persistent invading of provincial jurisdictions and its marked tendency to invoke the British North America Act to justify its misbehaviour, that is its obstinate refusal to exercise the specific authority provided for in this act. Once the need for a new constitution will have been shown, we are going to explain the basic elements of it and, finally, the need for that constitution to be approved by all citizens of the ten provinces by way of provincial and not federal referenda.
With regard to the British North America Act, I would say, Mr. Speaker, that as far as we are concerned, we consider it as an act passed by the British Parliament in London. But that is not where the problem is. Actually, all the hon. members in this House know quite well that the statement of reasons is an important part of any bill since it is useful for the understanding of the legislation, but when it comes to a private bill, it is essential that all allegations in the statement of reasons must be confirmed by reliable witnesses. The British North America Act was a private bill with reference to the parliament which adopted it because that Act did not concern the whole of the British Empire but only the three colonies named in the Act, Canada which included two provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That act was also of a restricted nature because it applied only to North America.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that the statement of reasons or preamble of any bill is very important because the terms of that preamble must be logical, and in accordance with the facts and any bill can be rejected if it can be established that such conditions have not been fulfilled. We have dealt with that aspect of the bill before the committee on the constitution during the summer recess.
Let us consider now the first condition with respect to the preamble. The language used in the preamble is quite illogical. And before going any further, I would like to read the first two paragraphs of the preamble of the British North America Act, and I quote:
An Act for the Union of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and the Government thereof; and for Purposes connected therewith.
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion under the Crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom.
I am puzzled when I read "with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom" given the fact that we have been told in committee that the United Kingdom has never had a written constitution. The United Kingdom does not have a written constitution! I therefore asked how Canada could have a written constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom and 1 received no answer and I am still waiting for one. Do we actually have a written constitution?
Before going any further, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to define two expressions: One is "federally united" and the other is "into one dominion". Are these expressions synonymous or are they the antithesis of one another? In his legal dictionary,
Canadian Constitution
Bouvier says that the expression "federal government" means the creation of a union or a confederation of sovereign states by virtue of a treaty or by mutual acceptance of a federative constitution. However, Mr. Speaker, this definition clearly establishes that sovereignty must precede the creation of the confederation and that the federal union is possible only with the consent of the states cosignatary to that constitution.
Let us get back now to the expression "into one dominion". Regarding this matter, I would like to point out that section 18(3) of the Interpretation Act of 1889 states that the word colony means any one of the dominions of His Majesty. It therefore appears that a dominion was no more than a colony. Mr. Speaker, could it be that these definitions indicate that a federal union and a dominion are opposed in principle and that one is the contrary of the other? How then could the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick federate themselves into one dominion? Is there not an obvious contradiction at this point? We are then wondering whether the terms employed in the outline of the stated purposes are in conformity with the facts.
In other words, have the provinces really expressed the wish to form a dominion according to the federal principle? Apparently not. And proof of this is this statement of Sir John Bourinot appearing in Chapter VIII, page 125, of his book "Canada Under British Rule", and I quote:
It is interesting to note that in the original bill, the United Provinces were called the Kingdom of Canada, but in the bill brought before parliament subsequently, they were called the Dominion of Canada.
And Sir John A. Macdonald himself said to the author that this amendment did not originate with colonial delegates but with the imperial minister. It is therefore obvious that the British North America Act reduced our country to the status of a colony. Canada did not become a federal union of a confederation but a colony under the name of Dominion.
It now seems obvious that the terms dominion and colony were similar, that in order to have a federal union, an agreement was required among the provinces, that no pact or agreement was entered into by them. It was said that a federal union or dominion was impossible, that the provinces did not express the wish to become a dominion within a federal union. Following all those inconsistencies, I wonder how the appropriateness of the BNA Act preamble can be demonstrated. Furthermore, if it cannot be demonstrated today, how could it have been possible in 1867? Therefore, the bill should have been rejected.
In that case, we, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, contend that the British North America Act is invalid. And it is not the first time we make this statement in the House as, in 1938, the Social Credit member for Jasper-Edson, in Alberta, Mr. Walter F. Kuhl, raised the same arguments which were never seriously refuted. He reached the same conclusions as we

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
did. It is perhaps time the representatives of all Canadian provinces listened to those who are in no way responsible for the disastrous situation facing us today.
To conclude this part of my speech concerning the British North America Act, I should like to quote the evidence given in 1935 by Beauchesne, a clerk the Flouse of Commons, before a special committee on the British North America Act, as reported on page 131.
It is true that if we apply to the British North America Act the same principles that apply to ordinary laws, it must be said that this act does not constitute a pact between the provinces. This act was passed by parliament and does not contain even the substance of every resolution adopted in Canada or in London before it was passed by the British parliament which added to it some sections that the Canadian provinces had not asked for.
And further:
According to me, the Assembly should not sit in Ottawa . ..
-Outside of Ottawa-
... so that the federal authority will not appear to control or influence it...
The Assembly might also ask itself if it would be appropriate to change the Dominion into a Kingdom ...
Since 1867, provincial rights have given rise to much controversy. When a new constitution is drafted, it will be necessary, it seems, to amend the distribution of powers between the Dominion and the provinces.
As one can see, Mr. Speaker, 40 years ago such sensible men as Messrs. Beauchesne and Kuhl had found a solution to our problem. What devilish force could prevent the nations making up our country from developing along the lines of that solution? It is high time we asked ourselves some questions. At this stage, I would like, if I may, to ask the hon. members to give me a few more minutes of their attention, because I am coming to the gist of my argument.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I have demonstrated earlier that sovereignty was the requirement of those provinces willing to enter into a confederative pact or a federal union. But what is the meaning of that sovereignty? Here again, I will refer to the second volume published by the task force on Canadian unity, because, if I am not mistaken, it is much more for us than for any other that the task force has clearly defined the terms of the debate. If this dictionary is not used by the legislators who sponsored it, I sincerely wonder who will use it? So, on page 14 of the book Coming to Terms The Words of the Debate, we find the following definition of the term sovereignty:
Sovereignty came to mean the right of the government of a state to decide in the final recourse, internally and externally, on the direction to give to its own collective actions, a right generally considered to be absolute in legal terms.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress that according to this definition sovereignty is an absolute right. Therefore, sovereignty admits of no restriction or quantification. A province cannot be more or less sovereign. It is either sovereign or it is not. Similarly, if sovereignty already legally recognized has to be negotiated, something is wrong, Mr. Speaker. First, let us see if the sovereignty of the provinces has already been legally recognized.

In fact, provincial sovereignty is a vested right since 1867 and was recognized by all governments even up to 1942. In support of this, I will refer to the 1942 agreements entered into by the then minister of finance in the Mackenzie King government, when Quebec agreed to waive for the duration of the war its direct taxation fields which were its exclusive right. It says here, and I quote:
Whereas in order to allow for a maximum war effort on the part of Canada it is necessary that the federal parliament alone have the authority to levy directly personal and corporate income taxes... Whereas the Canadian government recognizes that the province, by entering into this agreement, relinquishes or waives no part of its sovereignty nor any of its constitutional rights, powers or privileges...
Mr. Speaker, I would emphasize this is a most important document in our wartime national history and especially in provincial history thereafter, and it specifies that the province of Quebec relinquished no part of its sovereignty. This therefore is evidence enough that such an absolute right was formally recognized to the provinces. In addition to supporting my suggestions that sovereignty has been a recognized right of provinces since the very inception of confederation, that section I of the 1942 agreements also explains why federal-provincial conferences have been increasingly less productive since 1942. The reason is the high robbery type of action by the federal government in refusing to give back the direct taxation fields borrowed from provinces for the duration of the war. And further, it took advantage of those new tax fields to get involved in matters of provincial jurisdiction such as education, health, agriculture and so on. Deprived of their main source of revenues, the provinces had no choice. They had to join the famous shared-cost programs where Ottawa was remitting one third only of the tax money it was collecting in the provinces, because it was either that or nothing. And what is Ottawa doing now? It is gradually stepping out of those shared-cost programs, leaving provinces with all the responsibility without giving them back the total fiscal points that go with it, those fiscal points that were borrowed in 1942.
Therefore, from that one third they were getting, the provinces' share is now reduced to nothing. Only yesterday, Mr. Speaker, we witnessed one such atrocity when Bill C-2 passed. The federal government got out of that two years before due date; it stopped helping the construction of a medical research centre, without any indication it was giving back to the provinces the funds needed to finance the whole of these programs. There are also measures such as Bill C-14, under which the names of 250,000 jobless Canadians were struck from unemployment insurance lists, and abandoned to the care of provinces-

harassing them and trying to provoke confrontations by all means.
To begin with, in 1973, this government launched an official language policy which was sound in principle but which was implemented in such an inconsistent and incompetent way, especially in the Public Service, that it sowed discord throughout Canada and pitted English-speaking Canadians against French-speaking Canadians. So, after having launched this stategy in 1973, the Prime Minister entered the second stage and began treating the provincial premiers as minus habentes at federal-provincial conferences.
In 1976 particularly, this same Prime Minister began playing with the idea of repatriating the constitution, one thing he knew Canadians of both British and French origins would never agree upon. This created confusion, Mr. Speaker. Only a small spark was necessary to set up a conflagration. And what could have best suited the purpose than chastising the people of Quebec by insulting their premier publicly, saying he was a hot-dog freak? How can you explain otherwise that seemingly irrational gesture of a strategist of the present Prime Minister's stamp? Furthermore, this increased his prestige among the English-speaking elements of the country who saw in him the man capable of subduing the Quebeckers. This way, he killed two birds with one stone.
Once again sensing the great danger that was threatening provincial sovereignty, we, of the Social Credit party, in conformity with our action in previous years, took the following position which was to become the basis for the constitutional policy of our party afterwards, and which I stated clearly in this House on April 9, 1976 in the following terms, and I quote:
We, especially Quebeckers, demand power of veto for our provincial government. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) with great interest, hoping that he would throw more light on his proposals. But I listened in vain. He made a long speech on our constitutional history and matters of sovereignty without, however, saying much about the motion he put before the House.
The elements of his speech are indeed worthy of a long debate, and doubtless there will be one some day. However, I am sure he will forgive me if I limit myself today to speaking to the motion. Mr. Speaker, what does that motion say? [English]
I think I should read the motion into the record of the House since the hon. member was not interested in doing so. Let me read what we are debating today:
That, in the opinion of this House, the federal government having taken advantage of the weakness of the British North America Act (BNA Act) to infringe on provincial jurisdictions and undermine the sovereignty of the provinces, has failed:
-to leave the initiative of constitutional negotiations to the provinces, in accordance with the spirit of confederation, by giving them the final say in the decision-making process;
-to discuss the introduction of economic rights for all citizens in a new constitution;
-as well to recognize that new constitutional arrangements may be ratified only by the population of the provinces through referendums held in the respective provinces.
At the outset I would like to indicate there are a number of things in the resolution with which the government has no quarrel and with which it is in agreement. Also there are a number of items with which the government is not in agreement.
Let me take the last proposition first, the question of a referendum as a means of ensuring that the population has the ability to decide whether constitutional amendments are accepted. This is not a proposition to which the government takes objection at this point in time. We have no position on whether a referendum should be used as a means of indicating the popular support for a series of constitutional amendments.
February 9, 1979

The position taken by the governments that constitutional negotiations are well under way, that the traditional method of finding a solution to our constitutional problems should be followed, and whether a referendum is required or indeed necessary by the 11 governments of Canada is a question on which we have an open mind.
As hon. members know, the Flouse of Commons recently gave second reading to Bill C-9, which is the federal government's proposition on a constitutional referendum. On that basis of fact, we are satisfied we will have that kind of weapon in our armament. We have not closed the door to the use of it for this kind of purpose, and indeed perhaps it could be used for this kind of purpose. But at the present time we have not made any determination. We believe the means of developing an amending formula would be a question of negotiations between the provinces and the federal government. At this time we feel it would be unseemly for the federal government to insist upon a particular formula for amending the contitu-tion and thereby imposing it on the provinces. In fact, what has been going on in the constitutional discussions held with the provinces has been a precise and detailed exploration of possible formulae for amending the Canadian constitution.
As hon. members are well aware, at the present time the legal situation is that if the House of Commons and the Senate pass an address praying that the British parliament pass amendments to the British North America Act, in fact the British parliament will do that and the British parliament will not look behind the address to ensure the provinces of Canada have agreed to such an address. Their position is that the power to make constitutional amendments affecting the division of powers is that of the federal government. That is the constitutional provision as it exists today in the British North America Act.
We have proposed a number of formulae to the provinces as methods of amending our act. I suppose the most famous is the Victoria formula which would provide for agreement among a certain percentage of the population and certain agreements by provinces in particular regions. As the formula works out, it would require the assent of two provinces in the maritimes, two out of the four provinces in the west, and the assent of Quebec and Ontario, mainly because of the manner in which the Canadian population is spread from coast to coast.
If one takes a look at the manner in which the population is spread from coast to coast, one comes up with an unenviable situation: approximately 30 per cent is found in Ontario; approximately 25 per cent is found in Quebec; approximately 10.8 per cent is found in British Columbia; approximately 8 per cent is found in Alberta; Manitoba and Saskatchewan each have approximately 5 per cent of the population; Prince Edward Island has .1 per cent of the total Canadian population; and the populations of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick range between 2 per cent and 3 per cent. When one attempts to find an amending formula which will be just to all components of the country, one will discover there is no easy formula.
Canadian Constitution
One of the formulae developed in the recent constitutional talks is what we have dubbed the "Toronto consensus" because it emerged out of our constitutional discussions there. The formula provided for a factor of 85 per cent of the Canadian population represented by two-thirds of the provinces. Also it involved two lists: a precise list where there must be unanimity when dealing with the question of natural resources and the amending formula itself; and a second list on which the second formula would apply.
We have had great experience in Canada with formulae to amend the Canadian constitution. What is the current status in terms of the recent constitutional conference? The current status is that the premiers came into this conference bound by the rule of unanimity. In other words, they would not agree on anything unless there was unanimity among the provinces. The federal government feels that on balance this is a policy which is an extraordinarily restrictive formula for amending the Canadian constitution.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext: That is the puzzle.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
I agree that unanimity requires perfection. We are human beings, we are not perfect. In some ways the hon. member is fortunate enough to come from a small caucus. He knows how difficult it is, even within his own caucus, to reach unanimity on many subjects. We on this side of the House know how difficult it is for us to reach unanimity on many subjects. None the less the premiers have bound themselves by the rule of unanimity. They have said in fact to Canadians that unless they can reach unanimity on all these subjects, they are not prepared to move.
I believe that if hon. members had looked at the results of the last conference of first ministers held on Monday and Tuesday of this week, they would have discovered that on almost all items we were dealing with a consensus of eight or nine provinces and the federal government. This is a significant level of agreement, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker. When you have eight or nine out of 11 governments agreeing on a series of propositions, that is significant agreement in principle.
I would go further and point out that had we adopted the Victoria formula, had we adopted the Toronto consensus, or had we adopted the American formula of three quarters of the states agreeing, people would have said this conference was a fantastic success because we would have had agreement on almost every item that was under discussion by the first ministers. In point of fact, because the provinces have bound themselves by the rule of unanimity, having said that all 11 governments must be unanimous before they will proceed the conference was seen as only a half success.
As a result of this rule of unanimity we must have more meetings of first minutes and further meetings of the continuing committee of ministers on the constitution. There will have to be a further meeting of first ministers, I would expect some time within the next eight months. At what time and at what

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
place I cannot say, but I would think that the continuing committee of ministers on the constitution, which met three times, at Mont St. Marie, at Toronto and at Vancouver, plus an extra meeting of officials in Ottawa, will have-

speechtext: Why don't you meet in Quebec City?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS

Roberval, perhaps, but Quebec City attracts me. To get back to the point, we will require further meetings and discussions to see if we can refine the proposals we have made down to the point where we can deal with them all in a unanimous spirit. I want to point out to the House that this is not going to be an easy task since there are provincial governments which disagree with the propositions that have been advanced because they do not go far enough, or because they go too far.
1 would point out to hon. members that the federal government on almost all items was part of the general consensus, and there was a feeling that the federal government, which had been considered to be too rigid in its approach to constitutional changes, had become much more open and much more receptive to the need for constitutional change.
The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) mentioned quite explicitly the Pepin-Robarts report. I take seriously the comments he made in terms of Pepin-Robarts. I used the lunch hour to go back over the propositions that had been suggested by Pepin-Robarts and to compare them with propositions that had been dealt with by the first ministers at their conference. I am prepared to say to hon. members that if they will look at what was discussed and at the texts they will find that in many cases the negotiations which had taken place on the part of governments before the Pepin-Robarts report came out were right along the same lines advocated by Pepin-Robarts.
For example, in respect of the Supreme Court, we had already come to the conclusion that the proposal advanced by the federal government in Bill C-60 was not appropriate and, that the proposition advanced by Pepin-Robarts was also not appropriate. Therefore, we are out of synchronization on that. But there were a number of other propositions, such as the one on natural resources, where we have gone far further through transfer of power from the federal government to the province than Pepin-Robarts advances. I think if you looked at all of these proposals, Mr. Speaker, and if you were to weigh them on the balance scale, you would propably find that we are, indeed, going along the same line as Pepin-Robarts.
I want to make it clear to members of the House that these actions were taken prior to the Pepin-Robarts report coming out. Furthermore, I think I should offer the opinion that, in terms of the over-all thrust of Pepin-Robarts, I feel that if Canadians could accept the analysis and diagnosis of Pepin-Robarts-not the recommendations but the analysis and the diagnosis-as a starting place for our discussions on national
[Mr. Reid.|
unity, and as a starting place for our discussions on constitutional change, we would for the first time in Canadian history have an opportunity, on the part of 11 governments and all people from coast to coast, to begin discussions on a very common basis in fact.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
Having been involved in these discussions for the last three months, that to me would be a significant improvement in the way in which Canadians have approached this very thorny problem
The second opinion I want to offer on the Pepin-Robarts report is that, on balance, I feel I could personally accept the prescriptions advanced by Pepin-Robarts. My interpretation of their recommendations is that involved is a transfer of power from the federal government to the provincial governments in certain areas, but also an equal transfer of power from provincial governments to the federal government in certain spheres, that what Pepin-Robarts was seeking was a new balance in confederation. Consequently, looked at from that point of view-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext: What have you to say about the statut particulier?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
I want to deal with that in a minute. If we accept that kind of idea of transfer, as I say, I would be inclined to go along with Pepin-Robarts, if the provincial governments were prepared to do so. I think the concept is ideal, and I would be prepared to buy the total package because I believe on balance it would leave the provinces stronger in those areas where they want to be stronger. We would also have a stronger federal government in areas where I believe the federal government ought to be stronger.
I want to deal with the statut particulier, and I want to deal with it in terms of Pepin-Robarts as well. I do not see where Pepin-Robarts recommended a statut particulier for the province of Quebec or, indeed, for any other province. What they did say was that any government is free to exercise powers coming under its jurisdiction or not exercise them, and the fact that it may not exercise such powers is not a reason for any other government either to move into that sphere or not exercise its powers. In other words, governments are perfectly able and free to accept or to reject the opportunity the constitution obliges. For that purpose, if you look at areas of jurisdiction that are under provincial control, including education and welfare, you will see that each province has developed its own idea as to how to cope with these specific jurisdictions, and that is all to the good.
I think it is unfair for people to say that Pepin-Robarts recommended a statut particulier, in my judgment they did not. What they indicated was that certain areas of jurisdiction should be turned over to the provinces, particularly in the cultural field, and if the provinces chose to exercise that jurisdiction or not exercise it, or to transfer it to another body, that was perfectly within their powers. I accept that as the reality of the Canadian constitution today.
February 9, 1979

For example, we have that relationship between the federal government and Quebec at this time, and I would give two examples. The first example is that in terms of income tax, the federal government collects taxes for nine provinces and remits that taxation to the provincial governments. However, in the case of Quebec, it has chosen to collect its own provincial income tax, which it has a perfect right to do. The second area in which I think there is a difference is in the realm of family allowances, which again is perfectly natural and acceptable under our constitution. There is no reason why any other provincial government should not avail itself of such opportunities as well. 1 reject the suggestion that Pepin-Robarts has indicated a statut particulier for Quebec.
I want to deal with the question of language rights for minorities. This is a very important subject. I am one of those who believes that this is a guarantee to the Francophones of Canada that their particular linguistic rights and right to survive as a cultural entity would be preserved across Canada. I believe that it would be a disaster for this country if we did not have those linguistic rights protected outside of Quebec, because it would force all Francophones into a fortress Quebec, which would be disastrous for the future of Canada. The Pepin-Robarts report states, quite emphatically, that the ideal solution would be to have those linguistic rights embedded in the constitution, a proposal which the current government has made in its Bill C-60 and with which we have no quarrel.
But in a burst of what one may call real politics, the Pepin-Robarts group decided that that was unlikely to happen and, therefore, second best-not First best, but second best- would be to have the provincial governments pass language legislation. 1 want to point out a number of things to hon. members in that regard. The first point is that the only province at this time which is bound by the constitution to provide second language rights is the province of Quebec. The second point I want to make is that there was an attempt in the province of Ontario to proceed with a statute dealing in general with language rights, but it was not accepted.
1 think that one can argue reasons for that which are understandable to people who are active in Ontario politics, but the point is that there is only one province that is bound by this obligation. It seems to me that there is no way that I as a federal politician can travel around this country and say that it is all right for Quebec to be bound by these services but that the Francophone minorities in other provinces should not have the same rights as the people who speak my language in other parts of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I disagree violently with the position taken by the Pepin-Robarts report. I think that they would have been wiser and would have done us all a greater service if they had stuck to their original proposition, which to me is the only valid one. It seems to me that in
Canadian Constitution
discussing constitutional renewal and the question of providing assurances to minority linguistic groups, we must as part of the majority not only be seen to be fair, but must make it clear that we are prepared to go overboard to be fair. Because all minority groups, wherever they are and under whatever circumstances they may be, have this fear that at any point in time the majority can turn against them. What we want to do is ensure that these people have their rights embedded as deeply as possible in the constitution, so that their rights are totally protected. 1 think that is the one area of substantive disagreement which I have with the Pepin-Robarts report.
I have one further point to make, Mr. Speaker, and that is to discuss the workload that the first ministers have undertaken. As hon. members know, when the conference broke up there was substantive agreement on almost every other item but there was not unanimity. At some point members of this House will have to face the question of what the rule of unanimity means and whether or not we are going to be able to move forward with substantive constitutional reform. For as long as one province has the power to block all others; then it seems to me that, while this may be convenient for the provinces concerned, it can have a deleterious effect on the country as a whole.
We as national politicians must think at all times of the welfare of our country as a whole. Those items which were discussed in the constitutional conference by the first ministers and not resolved will form part of the agenda of the continuing committee of ministers on the constitution.
In addition to that, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that the second list which was announced by my predecessor at the constitutional conference of first ministers in October would also be put on the table. I would like to run through that list to give hon. members an indication of the kinds of things that the federal government is proposing be discussed. It is important to remember that the first list which we went through on the division of powers was a list proposed by the premiers at Regina. The federal government accepted that list and also agreed to have intensive consultation, through the same process with the premiers, on the items in Bill C-60 with which they had some disagreement. That obligation has been discharged.
I would now like to read the second list presented by the federal government. I will read it out seriatim and then say a few words on each item. The first item deals with powers in the economic field to fight inflation, unemployment and regional disparity and to protect the dollar. The second item is the question of non-tariff barriers to interprovincial and international trade and investment. Third is the question of interprovincial and international movement of goods and services, including the right of passage of electricity, oil, gas and other minerals. Fourth is the question of barriers to the movement of persons for employment. Fifth is the regulation of competition. Sixth is the regulation of the Canadian securities market. Seventh is the question of marketing boards. Eighth is the problem of jurisdiction over minimum wages. Ninth is foreign relations and the role of provinces. Tenth is the question of the
3080

Canadian Constitution
appointment of superior court judges and of the setting up of federal courts for the administration of federal laws. Lastly, Canada's native people and the constitution.
These are the items that the federal government has put on the agenda for the next round of discussions, in addition, as I said before, to the items that were not resolved in the previous discussions which have come to a conclusion.
I think that it is clear to anybody who has studied the Pepin-Robarts report that this list published by the federal government back in October, 1978, is virtually identical in the economic powers that it wants discussed to those items enumerated by the Pepin-Robarts report as to where the federal government should have an overriding authority in the matter of better government and better control of our economic union. It is interesting to note that the policies that have been followed by the federal government and the provinces in these negotiations have fitted in reasonably well with the proposals and the general spirit of discussion which the Pepin-Robarts report recommends.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the constitutional discussions which began last fall have to be regarded as a significant step forward since we have had a significant amount of agreement amongst the provinces; and, further, that we accept basically the general propositions advanced by the Pepin-Robarts report in terms of its analysis and diagnosis of the problems which Canada is facing today. Even the Pepin-Robarts report said that while it could indicate general approaches, by and large it would be the government entering into negotiations that would determine how division of powers would be made.
1 would like to say to my friends in the Ralliement des Creditistes that I think they have proposed an interesting idea in that we should think in terms of using Bill C-9, the referendum bill, as a means of seeking the support of Canadians in the process of constitutional reform. This is a proposition which the government, up until now, has not considered. But I can assure them that it will be considered by the government, and I hope that it will also be considered by the justice committee which is dealing with Bill C-9 as well.

speechtext:

unanimity one last time in order to achieve a less flexible approach in our constitution".
So I do not think that the minister should try to pass it off that only the premiers were making that claim to unanimity. That, indeed, was the position of the Prime Minister. speechtext:
The member for Gloucester, even though he has perhaps intimated otherwise before, has now verified the position and has said no.
Sir, 1 would like to address some remarks to the motion which has been put forward today by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). I may say that the motion as put forward by the member for Roberval is one which we in this party reject, because the suggestion in that motion really runs counter to our system of federalism. If it was carried to its logical conclusion, it could emasculate the central government and, indeed, the parliament of Canada, by leaving the final decision-making power in all things up to the provinces. Quite frankly, I was not elected to parliament to participate in its demise, and neither do I think were the members of the party that introduced this motion.
This motion does not call merely for changes to our present system of federalism in order to improve it. Rather, it suggests such drastic changes to our system of interrelated governments that we would end up little more than a very loose alliance of more or less autonomous units strung out across the country.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I agree that the federal government acted too often in provincial areas of jurisdiction. That complaint was well expressed by the provinces themselves in the past and it should be of interest to anyone concerned with the political situation in Canada. However, the solution to those problems is not to lower the central government position to one of janitor in the present confederation. 1 think that would be going too far in the other direction.

There is the problem. It is right to ask what we can do now to put it right; but the answers will not come without a proper analysis of where the problem lies, and that proper analysis is something we have not had, either from the government or, as this motion shows, from the Social Credit party today.
That analysis of where our problems actually exist must incorporate an understanding of the reasons for the friction
Canadian Constitution
and the tensions which have developed between the federal government and all the provincial governments, something that has been developing over many years and certainly escalating over the past 30 years.
Perhaps the easiest way to understand what I am talking about is to look at the Canada that we had 30 or 40 years ago as it emerged from the Second World War, because that war fundamentally changed our federal system, making the federal government more powerful than ever before. The government assumed sweeping powers to regulate our economy and nationalize our resources for the war and, perhaps more importantly, for the future of our federal system. The federal government took over the great bulk of the tax resources in order to finance the military effort and that, sir, indeed was appropriate during that period of time-during the war.
But in peacetime such a system was no longer adequate for Canada's needs. We came out of the war with a very centralized system. The federal government was big. It had developed a large bureaucracy. The federal government was rich; it controlled the bulk of our tax dollars. And the federal government was already becoming arrogant; it increasingly assumed that it knew best, that the provinces were children needing strict parental guidance, that Canada would be strong only if the federal government was bigger than anyone else.
This approach, appropriate in the war years, could not last. Why is that? The critical problems facing Canada in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s-the major areas in which Canadians were demanding action-fell within provincial jurisdiction, according to the BNA Act. There were better health and social services, enhanced education opportunities for our children, better housing and modern highways, planned urban growth and rapid transit, development of our natural resources and careful management of our environment. The list seemed endless.
These were the urgent problems of a mature and industrial society and they fell either exclusively or predominantly within provincial jurisdiction. As a result the Canadian federal system became increasingly out of balance. Big government was in Ottawa and most of the tax dollars were there, but the real problems were in the constitutional laps of the provinces. The result was perhaps inevitable; tension, frustration and anger.
Much of our troubled constitutional history of the last 20 years has been essentially a search for a new balance, a new equilibrium between federal and provincial governments. Because of its cultural distinctiveness, Quebec pushed forward more vigorously in this search. But many of the fundamental, underlying problems and frustrations are shared by all provinces.
The tensions as I have observed them have been particularly noticeable recently in two fields: health and social services, and natural resources. In the case of health and social services the federal government, perhaps unwittingly, helped to plant the seed of provincial challenge. In the 1950s and 1960s Ottawa

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
used conditional grants to cajole and prod the provinces into big programs, such as hospitalization and medicare. As a consequence the provinces had developed the expertise, the administrative capability and the self-confidence with which to challenge the view that Ottawa knew what was best for them. Conflict followed, as night follows day. The new financial arrangements between the two levels of government in this area reflect one fundamental fact: the provinces are increasingly insisting on their right to determine their own priorities and policy.
I mentioned natural resources as a second area of tension. The worldwide explosive growth in demand for resources over the last decades, a growth dramatized by the energy crisis of the 1970s, has presented Canada with both challenges and opportunities. But given the very important powers over natural resources allocated to the provinces by the British North America Act, a critical aspect of Canada's well-being depends on the skill and wisdom with which provincial governments approach resources issues. The federal government can no longer presume to be the unchallenged guardian of our economic future. There must be joint co-operation.
Canada today is very different from the Canada of 1945. It is important that we understand the forces of change. The linguistic and cultural resurgence of French Canada is one central force, but the emergence of broader provincial responsibilities is another, which has too often been overlooked. [Translation]
One thing is certain, a strong and united Canada will have to find a new balance between the jurisdictions of both levels of government. We need to change our institutions at the federal level. Changes are also necessary in the distribution of powers, but it is also important to have a behavioural change in Ottawa. In the past, the relations between Ottawa and the other partners in confederation were too often marked by paternalistic and superior attitude. It is necessary to have those relations directed towards mutual respect in the future. [English]
What is necessary is a new balance, a new equilibrium between the federal and provincial governments. Mention has been made in this debate today of the recently released report of the Task Force on Canadian Unity. It has some very imaginative and workable proposals that would move in the direction of which I speak. Not all of the proposals in it can be or will be agreed to, but the emphasis that that report has placed on regional aspirations and power-sharing open up options that have long been closed in the mind of the current government. Many of the options that the task force speaks about were available a decade ago when relations between the federal government and the provinces were much less contentious. For instance, policies for opting out of federal-provincial agreements or for accommodating the distinct responsibilities of any province could have acted as safety valves in the growing federal-provincial conflict. But the valves were shut, the doors were closed and the country was directed down one corridor and one corridor only by a prime minister convinced,

in spite of the danger signals, that his way was the only way. The lack of these safety valves has resulted in compression of the tensions and resentment; compression to the point of explosion.
The Pepin-Robarts report suggests opening doors that long have been closed-the doors of regional expression, of more provincial input at the centre and less control of the regions. Above all, it reiterates the definitive characteristic of any federal system. They say that the definitive characteristic of any federal system is-and I hope all of us would agree with this-
-the equality of status, under the constitution, of the two orders of government-
This is a characteristic which precludes unilateral action by the federal government in matters that concern the provinces, something of which we have seen all too much in the past decade.
[ Translation]
The Pepin-Robarts task force stresses in its report the two distinctive features in this country: cultural dualism and regionalism. Those characteristics, which are often seen as negative realities, should and must be dealt with in a positive manner. As it is said in the report, we should learn to adapt ourselves better to them, to subscribe to them, to provide in Canada as a whole such opportunities for action that everyone will be able to take advantage of them.

I want to look particularly at the question of regionalism which the task force has identified as one of the major sources of tension in the country, but one with great potential for strengthening the country over-all. Regionalism is given two dimensions, and properly so. The two dimensions that are identified are the cultural dimension and the economic dimension of regionalism. The report recognizes that the powers necessary to reinforce the positive aspects of the cultural dimension can best be handled by the provinces. They make certain suggestions along that line. Similarly it recognizes that the powers necessary to reduce the negative aspects of economic dimensions are regionalism, that regional disparity can best be handled by the federal government, and it recommends a strengthening of that role. That, sir, is the kind of balance that we must be seeking in this country so that federalism does operate better.
However, the reconciliation of regional interests will only come about with a central government that is sensitive to regional needs: sensitive to the fact that restraint measures dreamed up in Ottawa and uniformly applied can cripple the weaker provinces; or that indiscriminate regulation of resource industries without regard to regulations in the provinces, where much of the responsibility truly falls, can regulate those industries right out of existence. The lack of such sensitivity in Ottawa is the root cause of many of the stresses and strains in our federal system. We will not have a strong Canada until that essential sensitivity is reintroduced.
February 9, 1979

To become more sensitive to the needs of the provinces is not to weaken the central government to the point where we give up the dream of a Canada of shared interests and mutual responsibilities. Rather, it is to build on those shared interests and responsibilities. It is to reconcile the dual impulses of a strong united Canada and strong, diverse regions within the institutions and processes of the central government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
The motion being debated today seems quite appropriate to me in this age of redefinition of the powers under our constitution. Given the present political instability and economic insecurity, there is no doubt that solving that problem could result in true national harmony which can still be achieved if we use the appropriate means.
Today I would like to draw the attention of the House to one of the priority aspects of the solution to the constitutional problem, an aspect that is unfortunately forgotten too often in the debate. To prevent errors of interpretation I will refer to

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
the document entitled Coming to Terms released a few days ago by the Task Force on Canadian Unity.
Here are the terms used by the task force to define the word "constitution", and I quote:
(2)	the definition of the principal organs of government in all four branches- the legislative, the executive, the judicial and the administrative-their composition, functions, powers and limitations:
(3)	the distribution and the co-ordination of powers between the two orders of government if the form of government is a federal one;
(4)	the definition of relationship between the governors and the governed, particularly the rights of the latter.
The Task Force on Canadian Unity does say that a constitution includes in particular the rights of the governed, the rights of the citizens. That is quite obvious and logical since the human being is the most important creature in any society and any society is there to serve the interests of the people it includes. When you talk about basic human rights, everybody agrees about the following definition: A society must be organized so as to allow the enjoyment of such basic rights as the right to decent standards of living, health and most fundamental freedoms.
All this is included one way or another in the Bill of Rights and other statutes. For its part, the constitution does not mention these rights even though they are quite important. For too many people, these rights have remained theoretical because they had no access to them, and this is the main thrust of my intervention. The use of these rights and their accessibility cannot be fully recognized in practice if the people do not have the necessary financial means. In proof of this, one only has to look at the figures quoted by the Senate Committe on Poverty in December, 1978 which showed a disastrous financial situation for a large number of people in Canada, In 1977, 882,000 single persons, or 42.9 per cent of people in this category, were below the poverty line, 1,288,000 families of two or more, or 21.5 per cent of Canadian families, were living below the poverty line. If one considers that the average Canadian family has four members, this means that 6,034,000 people were living below the poverty line in Canada.
To live below the poverty line means that you are deprived of all the required health services, the necessary food products, decent housing, proper clothing, and numerous services which are essential to the exercise of basic freedoms and to happiness, which means that you are denied basic human rights in a normal and modern society. I want today to emphasize the fact that if the constitution must guarantee basic rights, it must also guarantee the possibility to exercise these rights. Any constitution will remain theoretical and lead to the present confrontation if it does not guarantee economic rights for individuals, rights which are clearly set forth in the provisions of the constitution so that no member of society, and especially no government, can dismiss their basic commitments.
When we talk about the basic human rights, that is food, housing, clothing, heating, health, and so on, we are talking

about things that are essential to life and about the production of goods and services, and therefore about costs, prices, purchasing power and income. We are therefore talking about money and finance. It is quite easy to understand that the possibility to exercise these basic human rights is dependent upon the effectiveness of the financial system.
Fet us see in this British North America Act which is considered as our constitution, how the financial system is dealt with regarding its functions as an enabling agent of the exercise of our basic rights. Section 53 deals with appropriation and tax bills. Section 91 deals with the Canadian parliament's responsibility over the public debt, the raising of money, the currency and the coinage, the banks and paper issue of money, and the interest on money. Section 92 deals with the provincial legislature's responsibility over direct taxation, the borrowing of money on the sole credit of the province. A great many sections deal with interests, provincial public debts, consolidated revenue funds, the transfer of the assets and the liabilities of the provinces, the responsibility of Canada over the debts of the provinces and the raising of taxes and so on. In this document which we consider as our constitution, no mention is made whatsoever of the rights of the citizens and, above all, the latter are not even guaranteed a single way of exercising such rights.
There is reference to the right of the government to borrow, to tax, to transfer debts and therefore the right of the governments to last and ensure their own subsistence, and finance their administration be it good or bad through the taxpayers. The future constitution of Canada which will have to emerge from the current debates will have to acknowledge the sound organization of the financial system from which depends the access to basic rights. This financial system will have to be recognized as the first essential public service, the one which provides access to all the others. The constitution will also have to spell out the responsibilities within that system and the limitation of its field of action.
Secondly, this new association which will emerge from a new constitution will have to establish its true sovereignty, namely the right of the people to their existence, to fundamental liberties as compared to other countries, to decent living conditions and these rights as well as those of the individuals will only be exercised if the financial system makes it possible.
The words "borrower" and "sovereign" are tantamount to an antithesis the elements of which are incompatible. A borrower loses part of his sovereignty which he surrenders to his creditors. He no longer is his own master. We have all seen what happened in the case of the cities of New York and Cleveland. When they suddenly are on the verge of bankruptcy, their creditors dictated their own terms.
We in Canada are heading for the same bankruptcy. Our governments are overmortgaged, a situation which is creating similar problems for the public.

February 9, 1979
I have before me a list of public debts. Public and private debts of Canadians in 1977

It is to be noted that these figures do not include the debts of all municipalities in Canada. And we all know how deep in debt our municipalities are. The federal deficit alone increases by $822,000 every hour. This is ridiculous. Interest payable on total debt in 1978
