This is where the present constitution has led us by giving us borrower status, debitor status, the status of seemingly prosperous people as in New York who owe the shirts they are wearing. Those figures show how much purchasing power deficiency our system generates relative to costs and obligations. The Canadian constitution should establish a Canadian financial system that would be responsible for the circulation of all the money and credit needed for sound economic performance. This implies that Canada must create a public financial service.
There is ample evidence of the current system's permanent divorce from current economic reality. Time has come to change that. And if an example were needed, we have the floating Canadian dollar. It is on a constant downslide.
I would now like to submit to the House proposals that should be included in the next constitution. A century and a half ago or even a century ago those proposals would have looked unreal. But modern times, our high degree of civilization, the high level of knowledge, the enormous productive potential, automation and cybernetics have brought us to the end of an old society concept and the eve of a new society. It has been proved that we now have the human and physical assets, the energy resources and productive capacity to enter into an age where the constant insecurity and poverty now rampant will be reduced to isolated cases rather than a system feature as is now the case.
The new constitution should include provisions for a national credit board responsible for determining the resources needed for the country to fulfil individual aspirations and for submitting from time to time reports on the efficient use of those resources. These reports would give an inventory of our society's assets and an evaluation of the percentage used. It is
Canadian Constitution
indeed important to know our potential, which can be made available to our citizens so that they can exercise their basic rights. And when we talk about public credit, we should really have a clear idea of its worth. Moreover, I think that the situation which makes Canadians run into debt with their government which is itself constantly borrowing from foreign capital should be reversed and that the Constitution should grant to every citizen the title of shareholder of this country. Therefore, in his quality as shareholder, every citizen would regularly receive dividends which would constitute an income supplement calculated on the basis of the net benefits of the economic association formed by Canada. This title and the privileges which would derive from it should be granted to every citizen simply because of his Canadian citizenship.
This provision would create a true economic democracy as the citizens would become owners of their share of the Canadian wealth and through the benefits they would realize, they would gain an ever-increasing ability to finance projects suited to their needs.
If this country belongs to its citizens and if this partnership is aimed at bettering the quality of life for everyone and providing more fundamental rights, it is only normal that every citizen benefit directly from this partnership. In the light of the foregoing, I should now like to make proposals which would enable us to achieve the goals pursued. The next constitution should provide that the primary role of a government is to guarantee by every possible means for every individual and family an adequate income so that they are reasonably well off.
The minimum income required to be reasonably well off could be determined on an annual basis. For instance, and this is one only example but a quite realistic one, it could be agreed in 1979 that the minimum "reasonably well off' income could be defined as the poverty line, as established by the Senate committee, plus 15 per cent. By the same token, the next constitution should provide that no person living below the "reasonably well off' line should pay any tax. However, it seems perfectly normal and in order. I cannot understand that the Income Tax Act should tax people earning $2,000 or $2,500 when they need at least $5,000 to $6,000 to live.
Those two proposals imply the setting up of an organization to set the minimum annual income required by single individuals and families to live decently and to exercise their basic rights. As a result of the present uncertainty, we have the opportunity of making our country the first modern nation with a constitution that really serves the interests of its citizens. Our country can lead the way for the whole world through a constitution based essentially on the respect of basic human rights and with very strict provisions defining the means likely to give access to those rights to everyone.
I would add that the new constitution should recognize that the government closer to the citizen can better serve him. In that spirit, with regard to equalization, a formula should be

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
divised under which each entity (each province) would provide to the higher level of government on a voluntary basis the sums required for the administration of programs for which they have delegated the responsibility to the higher level of government for a period determined at their discretion.
The Canadian people can give themselves a constitution fashioned to human need. For hundreds of millions of people living in poverty and uncertainty throughout the world, we can become, by adopting an original constitution, a source of hope for a better future. Because of its international reputation, Canada is perfectly able to do this. In conclusion, I express the hope that all those who will participate at any level in the drafting of a new constitution will consider my remarks, because I am convinced, as well as my colleagues from the Social Credit party, that those proposals might prevent disputes and confrontations. It is our duty to prepare for our future Canada a system designed to ensure a standard of justice under which human beings will have precedence over financial interests. Then we might talk about a just society.
I am pretty sure that the procedure followed up to now with a view to drafting a new constitution could be improved. One only has to look at the result of federal-provincial conferences to be convinced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FEDERAL INFRINGEMENT ON PROVINCIAL JURISDICTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we could have hoped or at least expected that with the departure of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) the Social Credit Party of Canada would have left the winding paths of ultranationalism and the sinister maze of cheap casuitry.
We must unfortunately admit that the member for Champlain, his hysterical and furious messianism notwithstanding, brought a minimum of consistency to the interventions of his party in constitutional matters. The fact is that the wording of

the motion now under consideration and standing in the name of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) is so confused and hermetic that I hate to try even to analyze its substance. It just may be that the member for Roberval himself agrees since not once in his intervention did he refer to it and neither did the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I cannot say I blame her.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that today, which is an opposition day, we have a motion dealing with an extremely important matter reflecting one of our major concerns, namely the constitutional reform and the direction Canada intends to give in the future to the reform of its institutions.
I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid) for the wonderful speech he made earlier today, in which he frankly explained the problems facing us and reaffirmed our determination to succeed in this endeavour which means so much for the survival of this country and its institutions. I particularly appreciated his reference to the report of the Pepin-Robarts Commission, and the way he cleared up any misunderstandings that may have arisen from the presentation of that report and the unfavourable comments it attracted from the media and the politicians. Above all, I feel he deserves credit for emphasizing the outstanding job the commission has done in paving the way for a better understanding and identification of the Canadian problem.
Having said that, I should still like to speak to the motion before the House today if only in an attempt to see how some of the statements it contains can lead to confusion and in fact mislead Canadians. To my mind, the motion can be divided, at least at first glance that is what I gathered, into four parts. First, the introduction, where on the basis of the so-called weaknesses of our constitutional acts, and I suppose the British North America Act of 1867 is being referred to here, a denunciation is made of the outrageous intervention of the federal government in fields of provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, later on I shall endeavour to demonstrate that this assertion, on which the whole motion is based, is completely false and unsubstantiated. On the basis of that assertion, the Social Credit Party of Canada, and particularly the sponsor of the motion, denounces three government initiatives or actions which, according to him, justifies the presentation of a motion, though perhaps not of censure still asking the government to act otherwise.
First of all, the motion claims that the initiative of constitutional reform should be left to the provinces, should be taken by them in accordance with the constitutive elements of the Canadian federation. So, the first question that comes to my mind is this: does that mean, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian state, that the federal government, which is also legitimate by virtue of our constitutive acts, cannot take the initiative of a constitutional reform and, as a corollary, cannot even, I suppose, initiate arrangements in its own institutions, within its
February 9, 1979

own jurisdictions? To me, the answer is simple: the British North America Act gives the Government of Canada-the federal government-full jurisdiction to amend its Constitution and reform its institutions to give them greater flexibility.
The third aspect in this motion deals with the introduction of the economic rights of the people. I wonder what the mover of the motion means by that, Mr. Speaker. In my view, there are two possible interpretations: First-and this might be in line with the options which the Social Credit party has been advocating for years-writing in the constitution certain economic rights such as the guaranteed annual income thus making it mandatory for governments to provide for their people's basic economic requirements. But-as we shall see later-these are not the only rights. The right to work is also very important as well as the right to form collective associations and many others of that same type. The Socreds are certainly not the only ones who have made such proposals. Back in 1967, the then Minister of Justice who happened to be the right hon. Pierre Elliot Trudeau, released a document called the Canadian Charter of Human Rights, which dealt extensively with those economic rights.
By the way, there were many meetings leading eventually to the Victoria Conference, during which fundamental civil rights and freedoms, including economic rights, were thoroughly discussed by a sub-committee made up of the ministers of justice who finally decided that, in view of the present situation, more particularly the nature of our institutions and dual federal and provincial jurisdiction, economic rights could probably be better protected, and every participating minister agreed to that, if the constituent parties, more precisely the provinces, were allowed to legislate in this particular area because the enforcement of those rights requires positive government action and, that is why it seems more appropriate to let the provinces pass whatever legislation they deem necessary or are under pressure to adopt for the protection of such rights.
My fourth and final point, Mr. Speaker, is really current because it concerns referenda. The mover of this motion presumably supposes, that the provinces alone which make up the Canadian confederation, can, through public consultation accept or reject constitutional reforms. He also assumes that the federal government has no right to consult the people and hold such referenda. Again, I think that, despite the reservations expressed by certain parties in the House during the debate on Bill C-9 regarding the scope of the legislation, the types of questions to be put, the various areas of consultation which could lead to referenda, no one I think has suggested in this House, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government had no constitutional right to consult the people either at the national level, from coast to coast, or within a province, whether on an issue of general interest to Canadians or an issue relating to the specific interest of a given region.
Canadian Constitution
And once again, I do not think that the fourth point listed in the motion is hardly worth mentioning except to say that the constitutional basis for the following statement, and 1 quote from the motion, Mr. Speaker:
... new constitutional arrangements may be rati Tied only by the population of the provinces through referendums held in the respective provinces.
-ignores the true nature of our Canadian institutions.
But we are left with the preamble of the motion and I will read it again for the record:
That, in the opinion of this House, the federal government having taken advantage of the weaknesses of the British North America Act (BNA Act) to infringe on provincial jurisdictions .. .
Mr. Speaker, I seriously question the historic sources used by the research staff of the Social Credit Party of Canada as a basis for that statement. Whether they be French-speaking historians to refer to the new terminology used since 1977, or English-speaking, or even American historians as Mason Wade, or even people who have nothing to do with North America and especially European historians, but to my knowledge, nobody has ever suggested that under the British North America Act initially has given priority to provinces.
And in that context, I could quote Mason Wade but 1 do not have the book with me. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will refer to the report of the Senate committee session of 1939, when the government had asked the Senate to prepare an interpretation of the Privy Council judgment on sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act on joint powers. I got out some excerpts from the parliamentary debates of the Parliament of Canada before 1867, that is in 1864 and 1865, and at that time, Macdonald had this to say, Mr. Speaker, and I quote from page 144 of the document:
But in the proposed constitution, all matters of general interest, all that concerns the provinces as a whole, will be left exclusively to the federal Parliament while provincial legislatures will deal with local interests which although they do not concern the whole Confederation, are very significant at the local level.
Later he went on to say, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
We have conferred upon the general parliament all the major legislative matters. Not only have we specifically and in detail conferred upon it any power inherent in sovereignty and nationality, but we have specifically stated that any area of general interest which is not assigned to local parliaments would fall under the jurisdiction of the federated government and that local matters would come under local governments. Thus we have given strength to the general government and parliament, and we have avoided this great source of weakness which has caused disruption among the United States.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the United States were then facing extremely serious internal difficulties following the secession war.
Does that mean, Mr. Speaker, from what was said by the father of confederation par excellence-and I add my own little touch of nationalism, by Cartier-does that mean, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Macdonald, soon to become the first Prime Minister of Canada, of the Canadian confederation, thought of
3088

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
something that was rather like a confederal institution, as it is understood today, or rather was it not straightforwardly meant that what was intended was almost a legislative union, and I use the word legislative advisedly, Mr. Speaker, because Macdonald himself wanted a legislative union, because he considered that it would allow better policy co-ordination in the interest of all the colonies in the British North America of that time, and in particular the opening of the west, the abolition of tariff barriers, the building of a railroad; finally, he did not see the necessity to give local institutions much more than a role of local regionalism befitting glorified municipalities, as they put it at the time.
Cartier could not accept, of course, as a Francophone, and as he wanted to protect the interests of Lower Canada, he said to Macdonald: Since we have to get rid of the Union because it is not working, that is the Union of Upper and Lower Canada, but since we have to try to keep the British colonies in North America together, let us do it but let us make sure that the institutions will respect the rights of the Francophones-and he was thinking specifically of the rights of the Francophones in Lower Canada. So, in spite of Macdonald's reservations, the principle of a federal union was accepted. But a federal union extremely centralized at the time, a federal union which in the mind of its designers, including Cartier, was to give the central government practically absolute preponderance. And it was only later, Mr. Speaker, with the pleas put to the Privy Council that that first concept of the Canadian confederation was gradually watered down to finally arrive at a federalism which resembles that which we have now because in its very essence it has not changed that much since the last decisions of the Privy Council despite a back and forth movement of the preponderance of the central government.
And in that sense, I would like to remind hon. members of the Social Credit Party that we are now, according to all serious analysts of the Canadian political situation, in a period where the pendulum is moving toward a preponderance of the provinces. For example, at present, if you compare the budgets of the federal government with those of the provinces, including those of the municipalities, which come under the responsibility of the provinces, you have a ratio of 1/3 to 2/3. Is that the sign of an extremely centralized federation where the central government only controls a third of governmental and "perigovernmental" budgets. I do not think so. Indeed, I think it is a very healthy development. I am not one of those who advocate, particularly in the Canadian context, an overcentralization of all powers. That would be contrary to the spirit of the BN A Act of 1867. That would go against the Canadian social and cultural reality, and it goes even against the Canadian economic reality which is based on regionalisms rather than true complementarity.
Speaking of complementarity, Mr. Speaker, if there is any direction we should try to give our efforts towards "re-confederating", it should be to take us back to the spirit that

prevailed during the discussions leading to the Quebec and London conferences. At the time a whole series of factors existed which made our political men feel the need to unite. Some of those factors were political, and strictly political. For instance, the union of Lower and Upper Canada was in a political deadlock since 1840, with a whole series of governments falling one after the other.
Naturally that state of affairs interfered with the solution of the serious economic problems facing the colony at the time, including the development of the west, the need for considerable resources to build a railway, the laying down of the substructure of a maritime transport system to compete with the ones that were attracting both goods and their transportation towards the south, the United States. Another consideration was perceived at the time, namely the danger of the United States taking over, because of their power, their numbers, the various colonies located to the north. But one felt the need to unite for another reason. For many years already, privileges granted to the colony by the mother country had been reduced to the bare minimum, with the repeal of Corn Laws and others, so that Canada had to turn to the United States to carry on the majority of its trade and establish its own tariff barriers. Finally, Mr. Speaker, there are many more reasons, but most of them are mainly economic reasons and one must say that the Canadian federation such as it was conceived by its authors did manage to fulfil the economic aspirations of the Fathers of Confederation. The confederation or the British North America Act such as it is has led Canada to its present economic development. It has allowed it beyond all hopes. Laurier's big dream was that the end of the twentieth century would belong to Canada. Already he had visions of promises out west. These promises have been fulfilled, Mr. Speaker, not only in the west but all across Canada. And now, even in the poorer provinces, we had hoped-

February 9, 1979

particular the fulfilment of Quebeckers since 1960. But we will have to go back to the mentality which prevailed in 1867 and we will have to find again what made us unite and the motives behind this union instead of looking for motives to divide. Let us therefore set aside our differences if possible, and I think that was the aim pursued by the Task Force on National Unity, and rather concentrate on what basically unites us. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure and great enthusiasm that I rise today to dicuss this government's performance in constitutional matters. Before getting on with my remarks, I would like to thank this House for this opportunity to resume the debate opened last week on national harmony. We, of the Social Credit Party of Canada have put forward a motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the federal government having taken advantage of the weaknesses of the British North America Act (BNA Act) to infringe on provincial jurisdictions and undermine the sovereignty of the provinces, has failed:
-to leave the initiative of constitutional negotiations to the provinces, in accordance with the spirit of confederation, by giving them the final say in the decision-making process;
-to discuss the introduction of economic rights for all citizens in a new constitution;
-as well as to recognize that new constitutional arrangements may be ratified only by the population of the provinces through referendums held in the respective provinces.
I do not agree entirely with what the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) just said, namely that he does not understand the motion; he may not understand some paragraphs but generally speaking, after hearing his speech I think he agreed that there should be discussion to improve the new constitution we all want, including the English provinces, I think. It is certainly a great progress because, like everybody, I followed the latest conference held in Ottawa, and I think considerable progress was made towards consensus. I would not say towards unity because some people there, and I mean some of the provincial premiers, skated outside the rink but those who wanted to stick to the subject, demonstrated at least a lot of hope for the next discussions.
What concerns me today about this question of a new direction or a new constitution is that the federal government has gone one step ahead of the provinces by saying that it would hold a referendum through Bill C-9, but that it would reject outright any decision reached by those provinces which might have their own referenda. At this point I am referring to the Quebec referendum, to the provincial legislation providing for referendums in the province of Quebec. The minister stated yesterday before the committee on justice and legal affairs that the federal referendum legislation is meant to be a
Canadian Constitution
reflection of the provincial referendum, that is of the Quebec legislation on referendums.
I suggest that if we want Bill C-9 to be a reflection of the Quebec referendum, then we are on the wrong track. Firstly, our referendum provides that the decision of the electors is not binding in any way on the government to act on a majority decision. This means that it is not worth holding a referendum if it is so vague that the government is not bound by the majority decision. On the other hand, the provincial referendum legislation, which I know by heart, having read it maybe ten times, provides that when the majority decides on a given question to compel the government to take action, it clearly states that the government is then bound by its own act to take action. There is a whole world of difference here. The provincial government did not leave itself much of a choice, but it has reserved the choice of the question, mark you. I totally disagree on that because the question should have been stipulated in the provincial referendum act. That is the way I believe things should have been done. I for one, had I been a member of the Quebec National Assembly, would have voted against the referendum bill because I think the question should have been included in the act, because the legislation related primarily to the people's decision on provincial independence, because when you read and understand the act the way it should be read and understood, you can see that such is its intent.
Generally, however, I think the provincial bill was more complete and more specific than Bill C-9 now before the House. First of all, the federal-provincial constitutional conference of prime ministers has just been held. Generally speaking, the main matters in dispute remain unsolved because nobody wants to yield. It is certainly not easy to come out of a hundred-year deadlock between French-speaking and Englishspeaking Canadians, Mr. Speaker. Many have come up against a blank wall. I am thinking more particularly of men like Maxime Raymond, Jean-Franqois Pouliot, Lionel Groulx and Chaloult.
All these people wanted nothing more than equality for Quebec. I would like to quote now a few sentences by Lionel Groulx which I read this morning and which show what it all means. Lionel Groulx said about French-Canadians and about the province of Quebec:
We do not want to take anything from anyone. However, we do not intend anything to be taken away from us either. We are not preventing anyone from living their own life, but we also want to live our own.
Everyone was enthusiastic when they read these fine words, but nothing much has happened since. Canon Groulx died at the age of 87, 88 or 89. He had been fighting since the age of 26, 27 or 28 for the equality of Quebec with the rest of the Canadian provinces, but not very successfully because he died before this equality that every one of us wants could be achieved.

February 9, 1979
Canadian Constitution
I believe that we must now discuss the means of achieving national harmony, and it is precisely in expressing and recognizing the linguistic, religious, ethnic and cultural mosaic of the whole Canadian people.
Later on, the House of Commons should report or amend the referendum legislation, which has now been referred to the committee on justice and legal affairs, in order to expand and clarify it. In its present form, this legislation bothers our minorities, especially in Quebec and certain other provinces.
One of my colleagues described today quite eloquently the tendency of the federal government in the last 15 years to interfere increasingly with matters of provincial jurisdiction. Indeed, in all federal-provincial relations during this period, the central government has kept interfering in provincial affairs. The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) referred to the circumstances which led him to defend provincial interests at the federal level during his 17 years in the House of Commons. As he said so well, the federal government has consistently taken over the taxation fields which are the most profitable. It has gotten directly involved in financing education and taken the initiative to implement our first health insurance plan while knowing, of course, that the provinces did not have the financial means to make the first steps in this field. To my mind, that is outdated and the government should have withdrawn from those fields long ago.
In the past, a federal government had succeeded in monopolizing the field of direct taxation during the Second World War. Direct taxation was then the main source of revenue for the provinces who had gradually, come to rely on it. The constitution had provided them with the power of taxation at the time of the negotiations in 1867, this was the least important source of government revenue.
So, the federal government took advantage of a difficult situation to rob the provinces of their only important source of income. Having grabbed those taxation powers for itself, the federal government proceeded to use its dominant financial position to infringe upon some fields previously under provincial jurisdiction. Those encroachments account to a great extent, for the present constitutional crisis and now we can see a dynamic move from provincial governments to repatriate within their jurisdictions those administrative powers that the central government took away from them in 1867.
This brief review of federal government action leaves me to discuss a new legislation which seems intended to make the tense relations between Canada and Quebec even worse. According to the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations, Bill C-9 respecting the public referendum on questions relating to constitutional matters should allow all Canadians to participate in the renewal process of the Canadian pact.
I think it is true, as the minister told us when he introduced Bill C-9, that the provinces will get involved in the referendum

as well as Canadians in every province, and that after such a federal referendum there will be a certain measure of justice.
By the way, I would like to tell you about an incident that occurred yesterday. I know that the minister is probably not fully responsible, but a small mistake was made. And I want to say that sometimes English comes more naturally. In the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, yesterday morning, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations made a statement in English. A member of the House, a Conservative member, asked if he had French copies of it. Quite honestly, the minister told him: I have no French copy, only English copies. So we adjourned the meeting since we did not have French copies. We realize that it is considered normal procedure to always work in English, and for the last eight years the government has shown an extraordinary openness as regards bilingualism in Canada. This has been going on for eight years!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, and there was no malice intended, but I merely wanted to show how hard it is to change 100-year old habits.
Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the remarks of the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations when he said that only the province of Quebec guarantees under a provincial act equal treatment to its minority. Why is it that the other provinces have not done likewise? It is only natural for them, that is why. I do not want to irritate or upset anybody but it is a fact that for them, of course, English comes first, and then we get the translations. I wish to congratulate my English-speaking colleagues who are helping us get equal rights for the French language, those who have helped us in the past in this House and who are helping us in committee in order to have the right to speak in French.
For a long time, Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit Party of Canada has been asking for the holding of referendums in order to seek the opinion of the Canadian people on major issues of special concern to individuals. We have asked several times, for instance, for a referendum on capital punishment. All our requests to that effect have been flatly turned down in the past by the government. We have also shown initiative on
February 9, 1979

constitutional matters by proposing a negotiation formula likely to foster understanding and public input. We have proposed the implementation of the required mechanism for the drafting of a Canadian constitution in the following order: first, every province would allow its population to express its opinion on the subject and would draft a master project stemming from this public expression of opinion which would then be submitted for public approval through a referendum. I am still talking about interprovincial relations. With a clear mandate, the provinces would then initiate interprovincial negotiations and submit the joint project for public approval a second time through a referendum. The federal government should stay completely out of these public consultations while reserving the right to discuss the final decision. At this stage, I would like to point out that if every time there is a provincial referendum, the federal government holds its own national referendum, we will then end up with a stalemate and nobody will ever make anything out of it.
Mr. Speaker, the federal legislation on referenda disregards provincial rights. This is mainly due to the fact that the government wants to get working tools similar to those of the province of Quebec with a view to ultimately thwarting the objectives of the Quebec government. The referendum would become the ideal instrument for federal intervention, enabling the government to impose its views to the provinces through the electorate. This policy would simply contest the sovereignty of the provinces. And yet the Pepin-Robarts Task Force on Canadian Unity in its report tabled in the Elouse last week recognizes that a confederation would represent, and 1 quote:
-an association in which sovereign states are joined together by a pact or treaty of international law, or a constitution, in which they delegate specific limited authority, especially in matters of foreign affairs (defence and diplomacy), to a central agency.
According to the definition given by dictionaries, this means a union between sovereign provinces. Today one is not even allowed to talk about sovereignty and to say that provinces can be sovereign, without being labelled a separatist because from what I understand, and I said so earlier and again I repeat, that when one quietly belongs to a majority, why bother to recognize a minority, why bother to recognize its rights? Again, why recognize the rights of a minority?
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, it is up to the citizens of the province involved to chart their constitutional future. Right now Quebec is the only province which has a law on referenda and it alone should decide its future. The residents of the other Canadian provinces should not be called upon to decide whether Quebec should stay within confederation. Of course they can try to convince Quebeckers to remain within confederation, but it is up to them to negotiate the conditions of participation for each and every province within this union so that every Canadian may feel that he can develop freely, and is given the same opportunities. So the federal
Canadian Constitution
government has no right to force the provinces to accept its own views on what Canada should be, especially through the technicalities of a referendum which might deny citizens-as I said before-a free political choice which they might have made with an overwhelming majority.
Counteracting the threat of a referendum by another referendum will certainly not enhance the quality of the debate on the constitution, obvious as it is that Canada would never allow the province of Quebec to sever its constitutional links with the rest of the country on the outcome of a referendum. Judging from all the speeches of hon. members, it is obvious that the referendum is designed as a reply to a specific threat. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) made this point very clear a few days ago.
Most political parties in the House have tried to convince us through statements they have made here over the last few weeks that the referendum will stimulate popular thinking and the development of viable constitutional options. It would be very easy to hold a referendum on the issue of capital punishment. The choices would be easy enough to make and the voters would be more or less free to choose. But in a referendum to change the Canadian constitution, it would be a lot more sophisticated and very difficult to reply for some individuals.
We must therefore devise a means of consultation which would be much more sophisticated and much more careful, which could allow people not only to vote yes or no on issues explained in advance, but also to take an active part in the process of formulating the options to be negotiated. In its previous contributions to the debate on this opposition day, the Social Credit Party has suggested the use of a better method of public consultation. This method should apply first of all at the provincial level, and later on, when the provinces have agreed on the change they demand, the federal government could decide. The bill on referenda reserves-

speechtext:
The bill on public referendums gives the federal government the right to hold such a referendum within one or several provinces or throughout Canada. This is, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, quite dangerous, because if the federal government is entitled to hold a referendum within a province, the Northwest Territories or elsewhere and since the cabinet is empowered to define the extent of the vote, it would be possible for the government to take advantage of the antagonistic interregional feelings now prevailing in this country to obtain the desired verdict.

Canadian Constitution
The present wording of the legislation would enable, through devious procedures, the government to remove the right of a province to take part in a referendum if a very serious opposition was expected. This matter may be raised since there is no reference in the bill to the criteria used by the government to organize a provincial or national referendum. This is why the referendum, as a result of the reactionary haste based on the Quebec referendum formula, could become a political instrument through which the federal government could substantially distort the wishes of Canadians or Quebeckers.
One of the arguments that was most often heard in the oratory battle undertaken within the House of Commons on the referendum issue suggests that the House of Commons could always protect the public interest during the debate period reserved for members by section 3 of the bill. This section 3, Mr. Speaker, provides for 40 hours of debate, if there is no general agreement on a given referendum question. I think it has been said here by some members that these 40 hours would be enough. That would justify setting aside this matter of the referendum intended by the federal government. Those in favour of this formula were saying that there might be a consensus of the parties in this House on a given question. Here, I refer, for instance, to page 2045 of Hansard of December 12, 1978, where a member was saying, and I quote:
If there is a particular referendum which we do not think is popular, the point is that we have the means in this House as an opposition to hold things up beyond the eight days. Indeed, if it happened that the government of the day, whether it be this government or any other, rammed through a referendum bill in the face of united opposition in the House of Commons, one does not have to guess what would happen. A referendum of that nature which did not have reasonable support and had to be rammed through would be defeated in advance. Any government would know that.
I agree on this point. But the hon. member is much too optimistic, I think, when he says that some day we might agree on a given question. We know the differences that exist between the objectives of the various parties in the House of Commons, and I believe that is a good thing, it is a beautiful mosaic, and that is what democracy is all about, but to simply suggest that we might all agree, one morning, on a given question, about which the government would like to hold a referendum, I believe that is mere wishful thinking.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would say that the Canadian experience shows that plebiscites were never in the interest of French Canadians nor of the province of Quebec. The 1942 exercise demonstrates effectively the vulnerability of this province against the rest of Canada about problems differently affecting the French Canadian and English Canadian cultures. In 1942, the province of Quebec was vigorously opposed to the conscription for military service. The Mackenzie King Liberal government used popular consultation to squeeze himself out of a promise made during the preceding election. They held a plebiscite to stir up the sense of pride of the majority in the English-speaking provinces, knowing quite well that the oppos-

February 9, 1979
ing voice, which was concentrated in the province of Quebec, would be overwhelmed by the voice of the English-speaking Canadians living outside Quebec. That will still be a danger in the future, Mr. Speaker. I am referring to that instance, though technically speaking a plebiscite is quite different from a referendum, in order to urge hon. members and all Canadians to be cautious.
Language and cultural differences tending to polarize opinions within specific regions could considerably undermine the rights of the French-Canadian minority and persuade them to reconsider their partnership in the Canadian confederation. The implications of that federal legislation with respect to the whole Quebec community suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the rights of a linguistic minority might be ignored by the central government.
The Social Credit Party is therefore urging the people in the provinces to get involved in this constitutional debate. It is for them to decide upon the contents of a new association agreement between Canadians which would not allow the federal government to freeze, by means of spectacular statements, our constitutional institutions into their present state.

Mr. Speaker, among other benefits the motion now before us has given me the pleasure of hearing the explanations given by the Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations) (Mr. Reid) on the last conference on constitutional matters, and also on certain aspects of the report put forward by the Task Force on Canadian Unity. It has also given us an opportunity to hear the excellent analysis made by my learned colleague from Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) on the constitution and the current state of the national unity debate. I commend him for that.
This was the second or third time I had the privilege of listening to an analysis by my young colleague, and I must express my admiration for the method with which he presented his subject and his mastery of it. He deserves praise. I also received confirmation of a fact we are all aware of on this side of the House. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) supports the claim made by Mr. Pierre Bourgault that the province of Quebec and the Quebec Assembly have the power to unilaterally declare independence and withdraw from our Canadian confederation. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands refused to answer a question put by my colleague from Gloucester (Mr. Breau). This question was: "Do you agree with Mr. Bourgault that Quebec has that unilateral power?" According to the hon. member the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had suggested that a federal referendum might for instance deny a province unilateral action such as, for instance, New Brunswick proclaiming French or English the only official language.
I very much regret that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands did not see fit to remain in this House to clarify her
February 9, 1979

point. A good number of Canadians will not know what to think on this.
We also heard the other hon. member read his motion. 1 have no intention to delve into it myself, since my colleague from Lafontaine-Rosemont did so in his brilliant fashion. I submit the motion is inconsistent and unfounded and, as did my hon. colleague, 1 wonder who could have put such a thing together.
This motion also gave me the opportunity to hear the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) make some allegations on the referendum and other aspects of Canadian society. He started by asserting that among so many persons who have studied the difficulties and so-called inequities English-speaking Canadians are alleged to have caused French Canadians, the efforts, representations and battles some Canadians are said to have made, he mentioned Canon Lionel Groulx. Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to attack the mystical Canon Groulx; however, I believe he had some responsibilities in the field of education, he should have accepted them, he should have won over my fellow countrymen and encouraged them to go into some fields that were practically unknown to French-speaking Canadians such as economics, engineering, geology and external affairs. He should have tried to convince them, especially the younger ones, to stop studying only for classical professions like law, medicine, priesthood, and look elsewhere. If that was the problem of French Canadians, I suggest it should have been pointed out, and Canon Groulx had the responsibility of selling his fellow countrymen the idea of taking up these careers. Still the hon. member for Richmond recognizes that the conference held in the last few days was a great step forward. Naturally there are so many differences of opinions, Mr. Speaker, that it would be illusory to think the minds will meet overnight and the heads of every province, jealous of the powers they received from their electors, will readily give up some of these powers in order to promote Canadian unity.
It is also an illusion to think that the leaders, those in charge of the federal administration, are also prepared to give up some of the powers which belong to the government of Canada. Therefore, this is why, and this is nevertheless an interesting evolution, Mr. Speaker, which gives us some hope, in the interest of the Canadian people as a whole, those in power, the leaders of that province will accept certain changes and mutations.
I come back to the point made by my colleague, the hon. member for Richmond, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members, with regard to the population of the provinces. In fact they should talk about the population of the country because in fact the people in Quebec are Canadian people, as they are in the city of Montreal. Therefore they are somewhat distorting the picture of our Canadian society when they talk about the population of the provinces. The population of the provinces is the population of the country. I might take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to remind my colleagues, and particularly my
Canadian Constitution
colleagues in the Social Credit Party, of our responsibility as hon. members in the House of Commons. I think that the mover and the hon. member who spoke next are not aware of that. In my opinion, the function of a member of the House of Commons is, in the first place, to look after the federal interests of his fellow citizens. Just as provincial members have the exclusive responsibility and obligation to look after the provincial interests of their voters. The same goes for members of a city council or of a school board. And each of us, Mr. Speaker, may rightfully pretend to represent, speak on behalf of, take action and adopt measures in the best interests, of the people we represent.
I do not quite understand, Mr. Speaker, why the Social Credit Party members will criticize the federal government's position and power. What I do undertand clearly though is how passionately the Progressive Conservative party is bent on decentralizing and weakening the central power, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has shown it. Mr. Speaker, we must see behind this an obvious scheme. Let us imagine for one moment that the central government is in a weak position, as some Conservative members would like to see it. It means that the whole equalization system would tumble down.
Of course, that is what the rich provinces could do, they would see advantages in not having to share their wealth with the have-not provinces. So as far as equalization payments are concerned, I want to warn the people in eastern Canada especially, including the people of Quebec, against falling into the trap laid by some Progressive Conservative members who are trying to convince and win people, and especially certain provinces, to move towards decentralization, which means the erosion or dilution of the central power and eventually the elimination of the equalization payment program which will result in low income Canadians being denied services either medicare or hospitalization of the quality which we are used to.
That is why I wish to remind the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that one of the Confederation's advantages is to make available to all Canadians, from all parts of the country, the same health hospital care, and educational standards and equal opportunity for post-secondary, under graduate and post-graduate education.
As I have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, let us remember the equalization programs and, all the programs through which the federal government is helping the have-not provinces, this would jeopardize them. Another hypothesis that could be considered is the one I am proposing: What would have happened to consumers in eastern Canada, east of the Ottawa river, if the oil price compensation program could not have been implemented because of a rift in the central power!
The federal government managed to convince the government of Alberta to share with Canadians in the less fortunate provinces the surtax Americans were and still are being

charged, which made it possible for Canadians in all provinces to pay the same price, for oil much below the international price. In the province of Quebec, premium gas sells for $1 a gallon, while in all western industrialized countries, and even Japan, it costs twice that price and even more.
The implementation of this oil price compensation program would have been absolutely impossible for Eastern Canadians had it not been for a central power which is exercized by the government of Canada and allows the redistribution of wealth in this country. I remind the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that every Canada-Ontario, Canada-British Columbia or Canada-Quebec or Canada-New Brunswick general program was established with the help and co-operation of provincial governments. And the priority of everyone of those governments is to set their own priorities and determine which program they want to promote.
So those are examples of the way the confederation of Canada works now. Although it is 112 or 113 years old, it works very well even if a large number of Canadians like to disparage the constitution, the central government and their country. Around the world how many people are thinking of leaving their country to make a new life for themselves elsewhere. Canada is the favorite choice of those who want to leave their country. And imagine those people, those Europeans and even the people of Africa and elsewhere who want to come to Canada, reading in the papers and hearing those unfounded criticisms about our country-it is really unfair for a country like ours which offers so much.
And the climate of federalOK-provincial relations is also often decried. I ask my colleagues, in particular those from the province of Quebec to consider the kind of climate now prevailing in the relations between the provincial and the municipal governments, and between the provincial government and the Quebec school boards. They will see that the present government of the province of Quebec does not even bother to consult anyone in its handling of public affairs and imposes its own views at provincial-municipal meetings while the municipalities cannot make their voices heard or suggest ways to best serve the public interest. The party now in power in the province of Quebec must really be weak, Mr. Speaker, if it so readily abandons responsibility for protecting provincial rights to the Social Credit Party, and in the light of the arguments raised by those members, it seems to me that they do not have good counsels and that their cause is in bad hands.
I would like to go back to the arguments and remarks by the honorable member for Kingston and the Islands to the effect that the powers that are being held and used by the Canadian government date back, for the most part, to the years 1939, 1945, and 1946, that is the war years.
So, since she referred to that period in Canadian history, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind all Canadians that if they really look at what took place in Canada, the national economy had developed during those years while the central author-

ity had grown and could take action or decisions without having to go through the process of consultation which can be quite lengthy and which prevents in reality the quick implementation of any change in the Canadian Constitution.
Mr. Speaker, certain people, including the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin), took the liberty of quoting from the report of the Task Force on Canadian Unity, the Pepin-Robarts commission. Of course, each one of us has a tendency to refer mostly to those things in the report with which he agrees. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I have certain doubts about this consultative process and this report, and this is the first opportunity that I have had to express my views publicly. To me, this report does not give a true picture of the Canadian reality because when such a group travels throughout a country, whether it be in Canada or elsewhere, to hear comments or criticisms about the direction that should be given to the country, it hears only extremist opinions. The middle-of-the-road views that are held by the majority of the people have not been heard, and the report reflects quite well, and quite faithfully in fact, the representations of the various movements heard by the Task Force. This is why, Mr. Speaker, we must take into account this weakness in the consultation process and realize that this can only give a caricature with extremist overtones and can falsify the image of the social climate of the country.
Aside from the activities of the Pepin-Robarts commission, Mr. Speaker, all of us in the Canadian parliament have the opportunity to travel throughout the country. For my part, I have had this opportunity since I was 18, or since 1940 or 1941 when I joined the Canadian Air Force, and I was able to meet Canadians of all ages, in every walk of life and in all the regions of the country. The situation and the conditions described in this report have been exaggerated, in my opinion. We could give numerous examples to prove the excellent relationship between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians.
I am in an excellent position to talk about it because I lived in several parts of the country when I was young, and I had the opportunity to see how Canadians in all parts of the country like Canadians from any social and ethnic group, and certainly, of course, French-speaking Canadians. That is why I view this report with reservations, Mr. Speaker, and I think, of course, that such an inquiry was not an exercise in futility, that it is an excellent way to know the extreme positions of our fellow citizens. However, I think it should not be considered as the absolute or exact truth on the situation of the Canadian mosaic.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in this debate. My intervention will not be lengthy. The motion before us appears to imply that the
February 9, 1979

British North America Act has allowed the federal government to infringe on provincial jurisdiction and that the federal power should be decentralized to the extent that the initiative in constitutional negotiations would be left to the provinces. I cannot believe this is really the intent of the motion because who knows what can happen once we start tearing the country apart. We hear much of this outside the House but I could not believe initiatives would be taken within the House to fragment this country and to break up a strong central government.
The constitution is a flexible document, which is both advantageous and necessary. It also has, however, disadvantages for a country of this size and of this diversity. This country is made up of people from all parts of the globe. They have various needs and aspirations. The British North America Act and a strong central government have served this country well for over 100 years. Certainly changes are needed from time to time, and changes have been made to reflect the needs of people in various regions and provinces.
The constitution is more than just a written document. It involves a set of relationships between governments and between the federal government and its people. Over the past 111 years this country has grown and developed. In 1867 our constitution provided a centralized structure, but since then there has been a gradual erosion of federal power as that became desirable and necessary to the various provinces.
The pendulum has swung back and forth. The federal government has taken power to itself when required in the interest of national security, for example, during the Second World War. However, never has the central government abused its power.

In a country as large as Canada which has a scattered population there is always a tendency toward provincial and local adherences, and rightly so. Communities adhere. This is what has built this country and made it strong, but that happened under the large umbrella of the federal system. There is, therefore, a greater need for a strong central voice, a strong national voice, and this is what has kept this country together. This is what built this country, and to suggest now that there should be an erosion of this strength or a fracturing of this umbrella is beyond my comprehension. I cannot under-

Canada is a land of diversity. There are various and conflicting interests, and the British North America Act embodies the hopes and aspirations of a growing country. Immigrants have come to this country in search of adventure, a home and peace. All of the aspirations of these people have been translated into the growth of this great country. This country has provided a home for people from all corners of the globe. This country is flexible enough to meet the aspirations of all people, no matter whether they be in the east, in the west, or in central Canada. The hopes and aspirations of all have been met. This country has everything one would require. Many people want to come to this country. Without a strong national voice there would be no co-ordination between the various regions. We need a strong national voice.
When the British North America Act was brought in 111 years ago it was visionary in its approach. It recognized the needs of the people, and it has served the people well for over 100 years. There have been changes, and changes are now required again because hopes, aspirations, and needs change. This act is flexible enough to accommodate all people who have come to this country and made it their home.
The constitution requires updating. Consequently we have before us a bill to strengthen this country, to reflect the needs of the regions and to serve the citizens of Canada. Constitutional amendments affect all Canadians, and I was very pleased to be able to take part in the debate just recently on the referendum bill which is before this House. From time to time dangers lurk. The unity of this country is in danger. Some want to fracture this great country, and 1 am pleased that we have a referendum bill before us so that we can consult the people and seek their advice on what they want for the future of this country by way of laws which will govern it.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak on this motion. In fact, I had no intention of doing so, and I see that it is 4:49 p.m. by the clock, but I wish to take this opportunity since no other member of the opposition wants to.
In fact, considering the number of members who took part in this debate and the concepts that were analyzed and put forward by the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada as well as by some members of the Liberal party, one finds that those concepts were very well documented. Unfortunately, except for one intervention from the Progressive Conservative party, from the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), I do not think that anyone from the New Democratic Party dealt with that issue. There was no real constructive input.
I feel this is a very good indication of the interest shown by the Progressive Conservative party, the official opposition party, in the constitutional issue. I am not surprised that they did not participate in this debate because the Progressive Conservatives have had some trouble to grasp the constitutional concept of our country as a direct result of their ignorance of what Canada really is.
This is unfortunate because when you come to a national crossroad, when you consider issues that are essential to the survival and the very existence of our country, you find that the official opposition party does not have the time to deal with those basic issues and to make its position known. We listened to the comments of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, but she spoke on her own behalf and did not state the position of her leader or her party. Besides, the points she made were not too clear. Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege of representing a Francophone minority outside the province of Quebec.
My interest in constitutional matters goes back a long way, ever since my early childhood. I received my schooling in the Ontario French educational system which as you know, Mr. Speaker, since you were a graduate of those institutions, did not enjoy the benefits available to the Ontario or even Quebec English-speaking students.
I learned to survive as a French-Canadian outside the province of Quebec. To understand exactly what was my status

as a Canadian, I had to be aware of the constitutional rights and guarantees provided in our constitution. It is obvious that some members opposite did not have that opportunity, because for them the constitution is merely a document. That is not the way to live. But for you and me, Mr. Speaker, the constitution was not only a document, it was a guarantee for us, Frenchspeaking Canadians living in an English-speaking province. That is why we have given it a lot a thought and that I still look into it carefully, because all these constitutional amendments will greatly affect the guarantees of the French-speaking minorities living outside Quebec, as well as those of the English-speaking minority living inside Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, let us not make the mistake of thinking that these questions are incidental. On the contrary, they are very basic. The question of linguistic minority rights was of paramount importance to our predecessors, the Fathers of Confederation, and they entrenched these guarantees in section 93 and 133 of the BNA Act. What has happened, in fact, is that we have progressed. In those days, Canada was made up of only four provinces, while it is made up today of ten provinces which cover more than 3,200 kilometers from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
As a French-speaking Canadian, I want to see entrenched in the constitution the recognition of what I am, of what a French-speaking or English-speaking Canadian is. I should like the confidence felt by my forebears when they left the province of Quebec to move to Ontario, when they left Quebec as French-speaking Canadians to become part of Ontario and go on living there as French-speaking Canadians, I should like that confidence, which was based on the guarantees in the British North America Act, to also be that of my descendants who may want to move to Alberta or British Columbia; I should like them to have that same opportunity, of living there the way I live in Ontario as a Francophone. That is why the matter of the protection of the rights of the minorities is fundamental to our constitutional discussions.
I simply want to repeat that I cannot perceive the survival of our country if the constitution of the future does not guarantee the protection of the rights of the linguistic minorities, and that guarantee should not be left to the provinces; it must be entrenched in the constitution by requiring the provinces, by constitutional decree, to protect the linguistic rights of the minorities. That being so, another issue also becomes very fundamental as it relates to our attitudes towards linguistic minorities. I mean decentralization. Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned that some would have us believe that Canada must suffer even further decentralization.
It was quite accurate when speakers on the government side indicated that the initial British North America Act was a centralizing document. When one reads the text of the British North America Act, it becomes quite evident that the central
February 9, 1979

government was going to be the paramount power. Under section 91 the residual power was left in the central government. There was a declaratory power which was left in the central government. There was le droit de desaveu, the power to disallow provincial laws, left in the central government. It was the governor in council, in the right of Canada, who was empowered to appoint lieutenant governors. Indeed, it was the governor in council who appointed all superior court judges. It becomes quite evident that it was a centralizing government.
If one looks at the constitutional cases, right up until 1896 there was even a greater centralizing interpretation given to our constitution. In 1896 there was a reversal, and we tended toward greater and greater decentralization when the privy council in Great Britain started identifying the needs of Canada as being those of regions and trying to distribute more and more of the powers to the regions. There is a coincidence in terms of that tendency toward decentralization and the question of the Manitoba school matter. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is present in the chamber. He will not recall first-hand the Laurier episode in 1896 which brought the Liberal government to power.
